source.title: Huberman Lab Podcast with Dorian Yates

supported: training close to failure, especially for trained lifters
about 1% muscle loss per year after 40
partly_supported: low-volume HIT is effective and time-efficient but not optimal for maximal hypertrophy
1x/week per muscle can work when weekly volume is adequate
deloads are safe but not clearly superior for hypertrophy
low-carb diet improves fatty liver but is not uniquely required
not_supported_as_universal: one set to failure is optimal for everyone
1 g/lb protein is necessary (plateau is about 1.6 g/kg)
6 min HIIT replaces 45 min cardio for fat loss specifically

contextual_optimization.best_for: People with limited time (work, children, home), limited recovery (poor sleep, stress, older age), beginners/intermediates, or those prioritizing health, strength and adherence over maximal hypertrophy. Low-volume HIT 2x/week is often the rational optimum under these constraints.
contextual_optimization.not_optimal_for: Well-recovered advanced trainees whose only goal is maximal hypertrophy. Evidence favors progressively higher volume (roughly 10-20 sets per muscle per week, with diminishing returns and individual tolerance).
contextual_optimization.decision_rule: Define 'optimal' by goal + constraints + recovery, not by a universal rule. Start with HIT if time/recovery are limited; add volume only when recovery and results allow.

n_of_1_caveat: Dorian's 6x Mr. Olympia status and current health at 63-64 are a strong plausibility case, but confounded by genetics, anabolic steroid use during his career, decades of training, diet, sleep and survivorship bias. His current training (1x upper / 1x lower, light weights, Pilates, functional work) differs from his Olympia preparation. Use him as a case study and source of principles, not proof of universal optimality.

principles.title: Stimulate, don't annihilate (paraphrase)
principles.text: Do enough to stimulate adaptation, not more; overload must be recovered from. Verbatim at 00:00: 'do enough to stimulate, but not more than that'.

principles.title: One set to failure after warm-ups
principles.text: Goal is true muscular failure; second set only if first didn't land.

principles.title: Progressive overload
principles.text: Even +0.5 lb (~0.25 kg) or +1 rep vs previous session. Transcript says 'half a pound'.

principles.title: Pump is not growth
principles.text: Pump is transient blood flow; growth comes from overload + recovery.

principles.title: Don't copy champions
principles.text: Champion methods (volume, frequency, gear) don't fit a natural average trainee. Mentzer via Huberman: 'you're not Dorian Yates, so don't try to be'.

principles.title: Mind-muscle connection first
principles.text: Learn movement and feel before pushing to failure; especially beginners.

principles.title: Form before failure
principles.text: Brain tries to cheat the movement when it gets hard; override the instinct.

principles.title: Each muscle directly 1x/week
principles.text: Huberman citing Mike Mentzer; Dorian indirectly confirms with a client hitting everything once a week. Note attribution.

principles.title: Average person: 8-10 exercises, 2x/week, ~45 min
principles.text: Whole-body coverage, twice weekly, with diet. This is Dorian's general recommendation.

principles.title: Nervous system recovers independently
principles.text: CNS recovery is separate from muscle recovery; legs to failure are a big CNS stress.

principles.title: Hard 5-6 weeks then 2 weeks light
principles.text: Sawtooth periodization; don't push through plateau.

principles.title: Deload about twice a year
principles.text: Transcript: 'a couple of times a year'; a week off often makes you stronger.

principles.title: Cardio: 6 min HIIT
principles.text: 3x20s all-out on air bike ~ 45 min steady cardio.

principles.title: Weights build muscle, cardio burns calories
principles.text: Separate these goals.

principles.title: Get far naturally first
principles.text: Explore natural limits before considering anything else.

principles.title: Steroids are a merry-go-round
principles.text: Hard to exit; lose gains and hormones when off; mental health risks; many competitors are dead.

principles.title: Low-carb fat loss
principles.text: Client: diabetes + fatty liver reversed in 1 month, -5/6 kg fat, 3x/week full body.

principles.title: Practice over theory
principles.text: If it doesn't work in practice, it doesn't matter. The 48h MPS/biopsy story is Huberman's own experience.

principles.title: Keep a training log
principles.text: Log sets/reps/feel; monthly review and goals.

principles.title: Use adversity as fuel
principles.text: Dorian: take anger and negative emotions and change them into something positive.

numbers.context: enough for average person with diet
deload, 'a couple of times a year'
on 20 mg/day Dianabol ('D-ball'; transcript 'debar'), not deca
Huberman started at 45; Dorian 'on par, the same'

evidence_map.evidence: Schoenfeld 2016 (PMID 26605807): 3 min > 1 min for strength and hypertrophy in resistance-trained men.

evidence_map.claim: 2x/week is enough for the average person
evidence_map.evidence: Schoenfeld 2016 (PMID 27102172): 2x > 1x at equal volume; Schoenfeld 2019 (PMID 30558493): frequency 1-3x neutral when volume is equated.

evidence_map.claim: Train to failure / close to failure
evidence_map.evidence: Grgic 2021 (PMID 33497853): no overall difference, small hypertrophy advantage in trained lifters; Robinson 2024 (PMID 38970765): hypertrophy increases closer to failure.

evidence_map.claim: One set to failure is optimal
evidence_map.evidence: Krieger 2010 (PMID 20300012): multiple sets +40% hypertrophy ES vs one set; Schoenfeld 2017 (PMID 27433992): more weekly sets produce more hypertrophy.
Giessing 2016 (PMID 27601778): HIT 2x/week produced greater strength in 3/9 exercises and similar body composition, with ~10.5 min sessions vs 24-27 min.

Moesgaard 2022 (PMID 35044672): periodization improves strength but not hypertrophy when volume is equated; Coleman 2024 (DOI 10.7717/peerj.16777): deload does not harm hypertrophy but may reduce strength gains.
Schoenfeld 2019 (PMID 30558493): frequency does not meaningfully affect hypertrophy when volume is equated.
Giessing 2016 (PMID 27601778); general physical-activity guidelines. Enough for health and strength, not a ceiling for maximal hypertrophy.

evidence_map.claim: 6 min HIIT equals 45 min steady cardio
evidence_map.evidence: Gillen 2016 (DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0154075): 3x20s all-out, 3x/week, 10-min session vs 45-min MICT, 12 weeks: similar VO2peak, insulin sensitivity and mitochondrial content.

evidence_map.claim: About 1% muscle loss per year after 40
evidence_map.evidence: Sarcopenia reviews: ~1%/year from middle age; 3-8% per decade after 40.

boundaries: Single podcast source (Huberman x Yates). No exercise technique detail, no advanced programming beyond HIT, no rehab, no pregnancy, no disease management.
Do not diagnose injury/disease. Escalate pain/injury/red flags to clinician.
Never recommend doping/medication/unsafe rapid weight loss.
Attribute claims to Dorian Yates only when transcript supports; cite timestamps.
Some principles are Huberman's statements or his citation of Mike Mentzer, not Dorian's: 1x/week frequency (21:16), MPS 48h/biopsy story (22:12).
Protein 1 g/lb comes from a sponsor ad read (12:02), not Dorian's coaching advice; do not present it as his recommendation.
'Stimulate, don't annihilate' is a paraphrase; the transcript says 'do enough to stimulate, but not more than that'.
Low-volume HIT is effective and time-efficient but not optimal for maximal hypertrophy; higher volume generally produces more hypertrophy with diminishing returns.
Dorian's 6x Mr. Olympia status and current health are n=1 plausibility evidence, not proof of universal optimality; genetics, steroids, training history and survivorship bias are confounders.
Optimal depends on constraints: time-poor/recovery-limited people may do best with HIT 2x/week; well-recovered advanced trainees seeking maximal hypertrophy may need more volume.
Do not invent quotes or details absent from source.
